newsitem.title: INDIA: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - January 17.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - January 17.

text.p: Following is a summary of major Indian business and political stories in leading newspapers prepared for REUTERS by Business News and Information Services Pvt Ltd, New Delhi Tel:3324842, 3351006, 3761233 Fax:+91-11-3351006 Internet: biznis@giasbm01.vsnl.net.in
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
TOP STORIES
The Hindustan Times
TRADE UNIONIST SHOT DEAD IN BOMBAY

Militant trade union leader and former Member of Parliament Datta Samant was shot dead in the northern suburbs of Bombay. His driver, who received severe injuries, was admitted to a hospital. The motive for the killing was yet to be ascertained. The police said it was working on several angles, including union rivalry and an old tiff with Samant's loyalist-turned-rivals. Meanwhile, the trade union party, Kamghar Aghadi, and Left parties called for a Bombay strike in protest against the killing of the trade union leader.
The Economic Times
APEX BANK APPROVAL FOR ECBS MAY BE DROPPED

The Finance Ministry is considering allowing corporates to raise external commercial borrowings (ECBs) under the $3-million scheme without getting prior sanction from the government or the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). The corporates would only have to inform RBI after striking the deal and comply with the regulations of Foreign Exchange Regulation Act. The government is also considering delegating the power, in phases, to approve all ECBs to the RBI. Currently, the RBI only approves short-term ECBs of less than three-year maturity and $3 million ECBs of three-year maturity also under the $3-million scheme.
PROVIDENT FUNDS MAY BE ALLOWED IN MARKETS

The government is considering a proposal to allow provident funds (PFs) to invest in the stock market. The government could begin by permitting PFs to invest up to one percent of their total corpus in the market, sources said. The move will inject 20 billion rupees into the market and boost the fund inflow. The new norms for PFs are being studied as one of the options for the capital market package promised by the prime minister.
BOURSES TO DISCUSS SUDDEN MARKET VOLATILITY

The stock market regulator (SEBI) has called a meeting of major bourses to discuss the sudden volatility in the markets. The meeting would also seek to conduct a quick ground level assessment of the monitoring and surveillance systems set up by the exchanges. The SEBI call came in the wake of a 154-point rise on the Bombay bourse sensitive index on January 15, 1997 followed by a net 190-point fall on January 16. The regulatory body also asked bourses to closely examine general trading patterns as well as scrips which saw unusually high volumes.
UNIT TRUST NOT RESPONSIBLE FOR CRASH

The Unit Trust of India (UTI) denied market rumours that heavy selling of pivotals by the premier mutual fund was responsible for the 190 points crash of the Bombay bourse. Though UTI refused to divulge their total sale, company sources claimed sales in the region of 500 million rupees. This was in contrast to claims by several brokers and market players that UTI had sold shares worth over two billion rupees.
HERBAL PASSPORT FOR VAN MELLE SUBSIDIARY

The makers of 'Fruit-Tella' and 'Mentos', Van Melle International, will be manufacturing confectionery and other products from natural ingredients in India. Some of the ingredients to be used can be classified as ayurvedic (herbal). The Dutch multinational has received approval for setting up a 100 percent subsidiary in the country. While other confectionery giants, such as Wrigleys and Agrolimen, failed to get approval for wholly owned subsidiaries, Van Melle used the ayurvedic products route to get approval for the same, industry experts said. Van Melle proposes to convert India as an important manufacturing base for exports to West Asia and America.
Financial Express
JINDAL DRUGS SEEKS DELISTING FROM BOURSES

Bombay-based SK Jindal group company Jindal Drugs sought delisting from the stock exchanges following its decision to cancel its 1995 maiden public issue and refund the entire amount to the shareholders. The move was spurred by its failure to get its ambitious 1.63 billion rupee ascorbic acid (vitamin C) project off the ground which was subsequently abandoned. Jindal Drugs also initiated arbitration proceedings in the International Chamber of Commerce against its technical collaborators, Noy Vallesina Engineering SpA of Italy, which it blamed for the project's failure.
ORDINANCE ON DEPOSITORIES ACT AMENDMENT PROMULGATED

The government promulgated an ordinance to amend the Depositories Act. The amendment would enable the shares of statutory bodies such as the Industrial Development Bank of India, the State Bank of India, other public sector banks and the units of mutual funds to be traded in depositories. The ordinance also amended various acts to exempt shares of these statutory bodies and units of mutual funds from stamp duty within a depository.
BOMBAY BOURSE INDEX NOSEDIVES BY 191 POINTS

The stock market experienced a historic somersault as the bulls pulled out in a massive selling wave. The Bombay Stock Exchange sensitive index crashed from a high of 3,812.31 to a low of 3,453.61, closing at 3,455.88 at a net loss of 190.85 points over the previous day's close. Trading in a large number of shares were suspended as their prices hit the lower end price band at both the BSE and National Stock Exchange (NSE). While the NSE notched a turnover of 23.05 billion rupees, the turnover at BSE was 11.77 billion rupees.
INDUSTRY BODY SUPPORTS FOREIGN INVESTMENT CAPS

A leading industry body has supported the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry's (Assocham) controversial report recommending a check on foreign equity in certain industries. The Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), which had raised objections on the issue previously, had promised to issue a white paper spelling out the imperatives of capping foreign stake in certain sectors. The apex chamber, however, did not issue any white paper after being criticised for following the pan-Indian section in CII, which has consistently opposed a majority stake to foreign companies. But CII seems to have become active once again in view of Assocham's concurrent views on the issue.
The Observer
DIVESTMENT PANEL NOT CONSULTED

The government did not consult the Disinvestment Commission before finalising the proposal of wholesale privatisation and outright sale of state-owned companies. In a departure from its earlier policy, the government sent a proposal to the cabinet for off-loading an equity stake up to 74 percent or outright sale, where desirable, in 11 public sector firms. Five of the companies listed in the proposal were making profits. Though the government had spelt out management and financial restructuring of state owned firms before going in for disinvestment, it had never mentioned outright sale.
WINTER CROP OUTPUT MAY DIP SHARPLY

The rabi (winter) crop is heading for a major setback, with almost a complete failure of winter rains, delayed planting and shortage of fertilisers. The Agriculture Ministry, which had set the rabi target at 94.28 million tonnes, has scaled down the expected production to the previous year's level of 87 million tonnes. But production may drop further due to a combination of negative factors over which the ministry has little control. The crisis caused by the lack of rain has been aggravated by the electricity shortage in the northern states.
DEVELOPMENT COUNCIL REACHES CONSENSUS ON GROWTH RATE

The National Development Council reached a consensus on the seven percent accelerated growth scenario, as envisaged in the Ninth Plan approach document. A resolution to this effect was passed unanimously at the end of the council's day-long deliberations with the prime minister calling for collective efforts to raise resources to the tune of 8,750 billion rupees for implementing the Plan. Endorsing the approach document, the states, however, said a number of issues relating to devolution of financial resources and powers remained unresolved and urged the commission to look into them while formulating the Ninth Plan document.
Business Standard
REGULATORY BODY TO FIX TELECOM TARIFFS

The Telecommunications Regulatory Authority (TRAI) will be the pricing authority for all services offered by the department of telecommunications and private operators. The redrafted bill, approved by the cabinet, has given TRAI full autonomy to implement the government's telecom policy. It will have the power to levy a fee on consumers and operators, and on rates determined in consultation with the government and the operators. Under the previous bill, rates and levies were to be determined by the government and TRAI was only an arbitration body.
POWER SUPPLY ACT AMENDMENT SOON

The government is planning to introduce an amendment to the Electricity Supply Act to clear the decks for private sector participation in transmission and distribution projects. The amendment will provide a legal framework to allow the private sector to invest in power transmission. It will also provide for the existence of a grid operator which could either be a state utility or a central organisation. The government would also issue tariff guidelines with sufficient scope to attract private investment in the sector. The amendment, vetted by the Law Ministry, is awaiting cabinet approval.
